dek: Set for 9 May 2027 in Hat Yai, Songkhla — southern Thailand's commercial hub near the Malaysian border — HATYAi21 is a single-distance 21.1km half marathon from a local organiser. Registration isn't open yet, but the date is locked in. Here's the early intelligence.
verdict: HATYAi21 is a refreshingly straightforward proposition: one distance (21.1km), one city (Hat Yai, Songkhla), one date (9 May 2027). No 5km fun run, no 10km bridge distance — just a half marathon in a city that sits at the crossroads of southern Thailand and northern Malaysia. The organiser, HATYAi21, is named after the race itself, which suggests a focused, single-event team rather than a big-series operator. Registration isn't open yet, and details beyond the date and venue are thin, but for runners in southern Thailand or northern Malaysia looking for a border-adjacent half marathon with minimal fuss, this is worth a calendar flag.

sections.heading: The Race: One Distance, One City, One Morning
paragraphs: HATYAi21 offers exactly what the name promises: a 21.1km half marathon in Hat Yai. There are no companion distances — no 10km, no 5km, no kids' dash — which makes it unusual in a region where multi-distance events are the default. [1] That singular focus could mean a cleaner race-day experience, with every aid station, marshal, and road closure calibrated for one distance and one pace spread.

The route has not been published yet, but Hat Yai is a relatively flat city built on a coastal plain in Songkhla province. Expect a road course through the city centre and possibly into the surrounding palm-and-rubber plantation roads that define the landscape south toward the Malaysian border.

sections.heading: The Location: Hat Yai, the South's Commercial Hub
paragraphs: Hat Yai is southern Thailand's largest city and a major transport junction — it sits on the Bangkok–Butterworth railway line, has an international airport with direct flights from Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, and is roughly 50km from the Malaysian border at Sadao. [1] For Malaysian runners, it's one of the most accessible Thai race destinations: a drive across the border from Kedah or Perlis, or a short flight from KL.

The city itself is a functional commercial centre rather than a tourist destination — don't expect beachfront vibes or heritage-quarter charm. What you get instead is a proper urban half marathon with good transport links, affordable accommodation, and some of the best street food in southern Thailand waiting at the finish line.
